questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: NUS has a very good academic reputation and an amazing selection of law courses in English. English being the offical language in makes everything easier. I had also heard good things about Singapore and had colleagues living there who told me it was very safe and easy to get around. I was also keen to see more of Asia, where I had not travelled much previously.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I absolutely fell in love with Singapore! It is so clean, well-planned and safe (and surprisigly green and pretty) and there is so much cultural diversity and incredible food! Everything works and people are kind and polite. 
My university courses were all very interesting and taught by incredibly knowledgable and enthusiastic professors who genuinely wanted to also hear the students' thoughts.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: NUS sent a lot of material with all the details you needed, but you did need to take the time to really read it through and make sure you could find it again, becuase there was a lot of admin!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Teachers and other students were quite helpful if you had questions about the course or Singapore. I was paired up with a local student buddy both by the university-wide global student association and the law international student association, both of those individuals were very kind to offer help with finding my way around and making me feel welcome. There were also some welcome events, but some of them took place before the semester start. Apart from that, you are mostly on your own.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I think NUS could do something more systematic to help visiting students settle in. In particular, there was very little information on exams and formalities, because they assumed everyone already knew.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Not easy to find something budget-friendly. Rent is expensive in Singapore and the accommodation that is easiest to find is usually more expensive. I used the resources provided by NUS, but ended up finding something reasonably cheap close to the law faculty through a colleague who lived in Singapore. I would recommend trying using facebook, but beware of scams. Also, I recommend not doing it last minute, if possible.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I loved living off campus - it is much easier to get out and experience Sinagpore, most places have air con and you're not stuck with a (cheap but not very nice) meal plan. You can eat cheaply at hawker centres (I did every day, it was cheaper than groceries). You do miss out on campus life, but you get to actually experience living in Singapore, which for me was a fair trade off. Public transport is really good (and affordable) so it is easy to get to class.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you have a disability or mental health condition, I highly recommend NOT declaring this in your campus housing application (unless you really neeed to)! They make you do two health checks with their doctors to confirm that you are "suited to campus living" and, besides the discrimnation issue,  this significantly delays the process of getting your campus housing result.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was stressful because there were a lot of steps and things to remember, but NUS genuinely does send you all the information you need, you just need to keep track of things. There is a physical registration with the university and immigration authorities right before the semester starts and you really want to turn up for that! In general, get the admin stuff done as soon as possible. Deadlines are strict.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There was a remote registration followed by a second registration in person. For courses, you apply for courses when you send NUS your application (in September for me) and then you can apply for more courses and / or drop courses right before the semester starts and again right after the semester start.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: NUS sends you all the information you need and you can find information on the various websites. If you need actual help beyond that, they're not very good at responding to emails, you're probably better off asking a professor or fellow student for help. The exchange students' Whatsapp group is also good.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very lucky in getting three of the courses I wanted through my initial application and getting a 4th course that I genuinely wanted right before the semester start.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Use NUSMods to check courses and timetables and remember the deadlines.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Law exchange students take courses that are available to both local 4th year BA students and MA students. The different levels are graded separately (we get lumped in with the 4th year BA students).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is a very different culture. All my classes were taught as seminars, but unlike back home they give you a grade for attendance and participation, which typically counts for 10 or 20% of your final grade in that subject. You can easly pass this if you show up to most classes and make the occassional intelligent comment in class. However, professors do expect you to turn up prepared and genuinely want to hear your thoughts on a subject. You also have graded assignments during the semester in most subjects, as well as an exam. The tone in class is more formal and they are more hierarchical (you call your teacher "professor", not by their first name). You are technically not allowed to eat in class, but I found most of my professors were fairly relaxed on this.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: World trade law, Aviation law and policy, International regulation of shipping and The law and economics of competition policy

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Aviation law and policy was really fun, especially with Singapore being an aviation hub, and professor Tan is the national expert in the subject! It was really interesting to discuss international, policy-related issues from a South-East Asia centered perspective.
Similarly, International regulation of shipping, because Sinagpore is a major shipping hub and it is a huge part of the country, and the professor is invites the students to conferences and such.
World trade law was also a super interesting subject, but the professor said we were his last class, so I don't know what will happen to the course.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were much more expensive than I's exected. However, I spent less on public transport than I'd planned, but I also lived within walking distance of the law faculty. I was surpised to find I didn't need to buy any books, but all the readings were provided electronically.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They had a really good range of extra-curricular clubs and activities and great facilities, but it was difficult to find information about these things. The one club I joined was quite serious, but I think you can choose to take that with a grain of salt as an exchanger. Also, it was free!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Lots of different groups for sports, music, dance, interests and cultural identities, but you have to look for it yourself

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I tried a hiking group and some dance classes and would recommend it if interested. It is a good way to meet people other than classmates, especially when living off campus.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
See the city! There is lots of history and atmospheric neighbourhoods. Go out and try all the foods you can't get back in Denmark - Singapore is famous for its food scene for a reason! I would really recommend the Botanic gardens when you need to find a bit of peace - it is a UNESCO world heritage site, very imperssive and very peaceful. There are also several nature reserves worth a visit.
Also, take time to visit some of the neighbouring countries. Singapre is super well connected with budget fligths to the rest of Asia.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it quite easy. The culture is more introverted, but people are very polite and friendly once you get talking to them. Be polite and respect the local rules and norms and you will be fine.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Make the first move and ask them for reccommendations or advice. They were usually very nice once you got talking to them, but often a bit shy. The culture is more introverted. The same goes for the Chinese exchange students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: You need to make a bit more effort to get to know the locals.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I loved the food and the mix of cultures. I really appreciated how genuinely considerate people are. On the few occassions I found myself in any way in difficulty, someoone immediately jumped in to offer help. They are also proud of their country and their culture, so if you ask for recommendations or information, they will be genuinely happy to provide this.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Don't get too hung up on reading everything for your courses. Remember to enjoy yourself and explore.
Be proactive at the beginning of your stay to find people you can hang out with.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring and umbrella, some ligthweight plastic shoes and a solid jumper (or be prepared to buy them) - it's hot, rains a lot and the aircon inside can be quite agressive.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to live in an Asian city and experience the a very different culture

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Homesickness - it sneaks up on you.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I highly recommend going to NUS and living in Sinagpore!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
